1317.title: Sindhi devotees of Nanak
1317.hook: many Sindhi families revere Guru Nanak and the Granth
1317.howItsDone: Some Sindhi families keep the Guru Granth Sahib in their homes or gather at darbars and tikanas to hear it read and sung, honoring Guru Nanak as their own, often alongside Hindu customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh Dharma in the West, and your line was newcomers welcome. Today, a devotion to Guru Nanak with its own shape, in Sindhi homes.

Before breakfast, a grandmother in a Sindhi family's home covers her head and steps into a small room kept a little differently from the rest of the house. The floor is swept twice. A cloth canopy hangs over a low platform, and on it, wrapped in fine cloth, rests a copy of the Guru Granth Sahib. A picture of Guru Nanak hangs nearby. On the same shelf there might be images from a Hindu shrine too. She reads a few lines of the Japji, then goes to make the tea. Nobody in the house wears a turban. Today we meet a devotion to Guru Nanak that has its own shape.
screen: `A SMALL ROOM, SWEPT TWICE.` → `THE GRANTH UNDER A CANOPY.` → `THE JAPJI BEFORE BREAKFAST.`

segments.voice: Nanakpanthi means one who walks on Nanak's path. It's a name used for people who revere Guru Nanak and the Granth whether or not they keep the Khalsa's outward form. In some Sindhi Hindu families the devotion runs deep. Tradition in Sindh remembers Guru Nanak's teaching reaching there through traveling teachers, and some Sindhi families came to hold the Granth as sacred and Guru Nanak as their own. Sindhi devotees gather at places called darbars or tikanas, where the Granth is honored and kirtan is sung, often beside images and customs from Hindu worship. A Sindhi family might name a child at the Granth, or read Sukhmani Sahib at a death. The Partition carried Sindhi families far from Sindh, and tradition remembers some carrying the Granth with them. Sikhs see this devotion in different ways. Some welcome it warmly as love for the Guru. Others are concerned about the Granth being placed beside images, since Sikh practice keeps the Guru Granth Sahib apart. Those conversations are real, sometimes hard, and they belong to the people having them. Underneath both is a line Guru Nanak sang, kept in the Sohila on Ang 13. In paraphrase: there is a light in everyone, and that light is the One; by its shining, all are lit. Nanak's word didn't stop at the edge of one community. It traveled to Sindh, into homes that keep it in their own way.
screen: `NANAKPANTHI: ON NANAK'S PATH.` · `SINDHI HOMES AND DARBARS.` · `SIKHS HOLD DIFFERENT VIEWS.` · `ANG 13: ONE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · then, large: `NANAK FOR MANY.`

segments.voice: Call to mind someone who loves something holy in a way you don't, a different ritual, a mix you wouldn't choose, and don't decide whether they're right. Just see the love in it, the swept floor, the covered head, the few lines before breakfast; breathe in that love, and breathe out, letting it be theirs.
Nanakpanthi. One who walks on Nanak's path. A name for people, among them Sindhi families, who revere Guru Nanak and the Granth in their own way. Today's word.
Your line: nanak for many. One light, kept in many kinds of homes. See you tomorrow.

1318.title: The Sikligar Sikhs
1318.hook: a community of metalworkers, many living in poverty
1318.howItsDone: Sikligar Sikhs work as smiths and sharpeners, often moving with their tools; some Sikh groups and volunteers work with Sikligar communities on schooling, housing and health.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanakpanthi, Sindhi devotees of Guru Nanak, and your line was nanak for many. Today, sparks at the edge of a market.

A grinding wheel spins at the edge of a market, throwing a thin fan of sparks. A man in a worn turban holds a kitchen knife to it, turns it, tests the edge on his thumbnail, hands it back. Next to him, a boy fans the coals under a small forge. By evening they'll pack the wheel, the tools and the bedding onto a cart and move on. Shoppers pass without looking twice. They may not know that this family's trade, in Sikh tradition, once served the Gurus' own armies. They are Sikligar Sikhs.
screen: `A GRINDING WHEEL AT THE MARKET'S EDGE.` → `A SMALL FORGE, A CART, A ROAD.` → `A TRADE THAT ONCE SERVED THE GURUS.`

segments.voice: The Sikligars are a community of metalworkers. Their crafts are forging, sharpening and mending: blades, locks, cooking griddles, iron tools of every kind. Tradition links their ancestors to the years when the Gurus raised armed companies, and remembers Sikligar smiths making weapons for them. Over time, Sikligar families took to the road, moving from town to town with their tools. Today Sikligar families can face deep poverty. Work is irregular, schooling is hard to keep when a family moves, and a craft that once forged swords now sharpens kitchen knives for small coins. They hold to Sikh identity, the Guru, the turban, the gurdwara, often while living at the edges of the towns they serve. Some Sikh groups and volunteers now work alongside Sikligar communities on schooling, housing and health. Guru Nanak, in a salok on Ang 1245, says in paraphrase: whoever eats what they earn by their own labor, and gives some of it with their own hand, has recognized the way. Hold that line up against the man at the grinding wheel. He earns by the work of his hands, as plainly as anyone can, and the Guru's words honor exactly that life. And the line doesn't stop at earning: give some of it with your own hand. That half is asked of everyone who hears it, the man at the wheel and the one handing him a knife. In tradition's telling, the Sikligars kept the Gurus' steel sharp in hard years. Remembering them now isn't charity from above. It's the panth remembering one of its own.
screen: `SIKLIGARS: FORGING, SHARPENING, MENDING.` · `TRADITION: SMITHS FOR THE GURUS' ARMIES.` · `TODAY: POVERTY ON THE ROAD.` · `ANG 1245: EARN BY LABOR, GIVE BY HAND.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE SIKLIGARS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who works hard and still struggles, someone who fixes, cleans, delivers or carries, and see their hands at work. Breathe in the question of one real thing you could do for them, a fair price paid without bargaining, a proper thank-you, and breathe out, keeping the answer. If you pray, rest on Waheguru.

1319.title: Lubana and Vanjara Sikhs
1319.hook: trading communities, like Makhan Shah and Lakhi Shah
1319.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Makhan Shah Lubana and Lakhi Shah Vanjara in the stories of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and Lubana and Vanjara Sikh families keep their trading heritage alongside their place in the panth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sikligar Sikhs, who kept the Gurus' steel sharp, and your line was remember the sikligars. Today, two traders the panth still names.

Guru Nanak sometimes speaks to the listener as a trader. In one hymn he calls the listener vanjaria mitra, my merchant friend, and walks them through the night of a life watch by watch, as if it were a long trading journey. What are you carrying home? The image would land in a world of traders: caravans of pack bullocks, boats on the rivers, goods moving from market to market. Some of those trading families became Sikhs. Two of them did something the panth still remembers.
screen: `MY MERCHANT FRIEND.` → `A LIFE AS A TRADING JOURNEY.` → `TRADERS WHO BECAME SIKHS.`

segments.voice: The Lubanas and the Vanjaras are trading communities, remembered for carrying goods across long distances by caravan and by boat. Both have Sikh families with deep roots in the panth, and Sikh tradition keeps two of their names close. First, Makhan Shah Lubana. The story says his ship was caught in a storm, and he vowed an offering of gold to the Guru if he came through. He did. When he went to pay his vow, he found a crowd of men each claiming to be the Guru. So he tried a quiet test: he laid a small offering before each claimant, and each accepted it. Then he came to a man sitting apart in meditation, Tegh Bahadur, who said, in effect: you promised more than this. Makhan Shah ran up to a rooftop and shouted that he had found the Guru. Second, Lakhi Shah Vanjara, and the story turns darker. After Guru Tegh Bahadur was executed in Delhi, his body lay where the authorities had left it. Tradition says Lakhi Shah, a carrier with carts and men, brought his caravan through, took the body away in the confusion, carried it home, and set his own house alight so the Guru could be cremated with honor without drawing attention. A gurdwara stands at that place today. One trader found a hidden Guru; one gave up his own house for him. Guru Nanak's merchant hymn, on Ang 74, follows the trader through the watches of the night to the journey's end. In the panth's memory, these two spent their journeys on the Guru, and it still says their names.
screen: `LUBANAS AND VANJARAS: CARAVAN TRADERS.` · `MAKHAN SHAH FINDS THE HIDDEN GURU.` · `LAKHI SHAH GIVES UP HIS HOUSE.` · `ANG 74: WHAT DOES THE TRADER CARRY HOME?` · then, large: `THE TRADERS.`

1320.title: Sikhs of Assam
1320.hook: a community in Assam traces itself to soldiers who stayed long ago
1320.howItsDone: Sikhs of Assam keep village gurdwaras in the Brahmaputra valley, say the Ardas and read the Guru Granth Sahib, and live their daily lives in Assamese language, food and dress.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lubana and Vanjara Sikhs, two traders the panth never forgot, and your line was the traders. Today, rice fields far to the east.

Rice fields in the Brahmaputra valley, green to the edge of the sky. A village gurdwara with a small Nishan Sahib above the trees. Inside, the Ardas is said in Punjabi, but outside, the children run home calling to each other in Assamese. Their grandmothers wear the mekhela, the Assamese wrap. Their fathers tie turbans. Ask the elders where the family came from, and the answer reaches back a long way, to men who marched east from Punjab and never marched home. These are the Sikhs of Assam.
screen: `RICE FIELDS AND A NISHAN SAHIB.` → `PUNJABI PRAYER, ASSAMESE PLAY.` → `MEN WHO NEVER MARCHED HOME.`

segments.voice: Start with the community's own memory. Tradition says soldiers from Punjab were sent east to help a king of Assam in a time of war. When the fighting was done, some of them didn't go back. They stayed, married into Assamese families, farmed the land, and built gurdwaras in their villages. Their descendants are Assamese by language, food and dress, and Sikh by faith. There's an older thread too. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur traveling to Assam, and a gurdwara on the Brahmaputra keeps that memory. So in the panth's telling, the Guru's footsteps reached the valley before the soldiers did. Being a Sikh far from Punjab has its own weight. A community like this has to keep Gurmukhi alive among children who think in another language, keep the rehat where few neighbors know what a kara or a turban means, and stay connected to a panth whose center is a long journey away. And yet this is also an old Sikh story. The Gurus traveled, and sangats grew in places where they stopped. Guru Ram Das sings, in a hymn on Ang 450, in paraphrase: wherever my true Guru goes and sits, that place becomes beautiful. A rice village in Assam is far from Amritsar. In the logic of that line, it's not far from the Guru. The Granth sits there, the Ardas is said there, and the place is made beautiful by it. Those who stayed far away didn't leave the Guru behind; they carried the Guru with them, and set the Granth down in new ground.

1321.title: Mazhabi Sikhs
1321.hook: Sikhs from Dalit backgrounds, heirs of Bhai Jaita, who served in honored regiments
1321.howItsDone: Mazhabi Sikhs remember Bhai Jaita, who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head to Anandpur, and the saying that the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons; they take pride in their service in the army's honored regiments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sikhs of Assam, and your line was stayed far away. Today, a man walking out of Delhi by night.

A man walks out of Delhi at night with a bundle held close against his chest. He keeps off the main roads; every checkpoint is a danger. What he carries is the head of Guru Tegh Bahadur, executed in the city. He is taking it to the Guru's young son, far to the north. Two days ago we followed the trader who carried the Guru's body home; this is the other road out of Delhi. His name, in Sikh memory, is Bhai Jaita. He came from a family that the society around him counted among the lowest. Today we meet the Sikhs who call him their own.
screen: `A BUNDLE CARRIED OUT OF DELHI.` → `THE HEAD OF GURU TEGH BAHADUR.` → `BHAI JAITA, COUNTED AMONG THE LOWEST.`

segments.voice: Mazhabi Sikhs are Sikhs from Dalit backgrounds, from communities the caste order pushed to its bottom rung. In the panth they honor Bhai Jaita as their forebear. As tradition tells it, Bhai Jaita reached Anandpur and laid the Guru's head before the young Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru embraced him and spoke a phrase Sikhs still repeat: the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons. Rangreta is a name tradition uses for Bhai Jaita's people. In a single sentence, a community the world treated as outcast was claimed as family by the Guru himself. Tradition remembers Bhai Jaita later taking amrit and fighting beside the Guru. Mazhabi Sikhs carried that courage into later centuries, serving in regiments of the army known for their battle honors, a point of deep pride. The story has a harder side. The Gurus' teaching on caste is plain, but caste prejudice has not vanished among Sikhs any more than among others. In places, Mazhabi Sikhs have faced exclusion, even in matters of worship. Sikh voices have long spoken against that, citing the Gurus. One of those lines: Guru Nanak, in Raag Asa on Ang 349, says in paraphrase: recognize the light in each person, and don't ask about caste; in what lies ahead, there is no caste. The Guru's embrace at Anandpur was that line lived out. The man carrying the Guru's head through the dark was family. The phrase the Guru's own sons isn't a compliment; it's a claim the panth is still asked to live up to.
screen: `MAZHABI SIKHS: FROM DALIT BACKGROUNDS.` · `ANANDPUR: THE GURU'S EMBRACE.` · `HONORED REGIMENTS, AND HARD PREJUDICE.` · `ANG 349: SEE THE LIGHT, NOT THE CASTE.` · then, large: `THE GURU'S OWN SONS.`

1322.title: Craftsmen and builders
1322.hook: Ramgarhia Sikhs, heirs of builders and carpenters
1322.howItsDone: Ramgarhia Sikhs keep the name of the Ramgarhia misl and a memory of craft; in some cities they have their own gurdwaras, open to every Sikh, and Sikhs everywhere tell the story of Guru Nanak and Lalo the carpenter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mazhabi Sikhs, heirs of Bhai Jaita, honored in their regiments. Your line was the guru's own sons.

Run a hand along the doorframe of the room you're in. Somebody measured that, cut it, checked it with a level, and fixed it in place, and it's easy to go a lifetime without a thought for them. So much of what holds us up is like that: beams, stairs, the bench outside the gurdwara where the old men sit. In some cities you'll pass a gurdwara with a sign that says Ramgarhia. That name has a story behind it, and a trade.
screen: `A DOORFRAME SOMEONE MEASURED.` → `WHAT HOLDS US UP GOES UNSEEN.` → `A SIGN THAT SAYS RAMGARHIA.`

segments.voice: Start with the people. Ramgarhia Sikhs trace their families to carpenters, masons, smiths and builders. Year three told how the name came from the Ramgarhia misl, one of the old bands of Sikh riders, and its leader, Jassa Singh, called Ramgarhia after the fort he held. So the name remembers a fort; the trade remembers hands that know wood and stone. Now the oldest piece. The janamsakhis, the stories of Guru Nanak's life, tell of a carpenter named Lalo. In the story, the Guru stays in Lalo's simple home and eats his plain bread, and turns down a feast from a rich official whose wealth came from squeezing others. The bread earned by a chisel, the story says, was the honest food. It's a story, told in the old collections. But Lalo isn't only a story. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak speaks a hymn to Lalo by name, during the violence of an invasion, telling him plainly what he has seen. Here's what he tells him, in paraphrase: as the word of the Master comes to me, so I speak it, Lalo. A hymn about where the Guru's words come from, spoken to a carpenter. Sikhs call honest work kirat. Building a wall straight is kirat. Fixing a hinge properly when nobody will check is kirat. And now: when Sikh families settled in new countries, some remember builders among them raising gurdwaras with their own hands. Every one of those doors was measured by somebody.
screen: `A NAME FROM A FORT, A TRADE FROM THE HANDS.` · `LALO THE CARPENTER, AND HIS BREAD.` · `AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK, LALO.` · `GURDWARAS RAISED BY BUILDERS.` · then, large: `BUILDERS.`

segments.voice: Look around the room and find one thing somebody made, a shelf, a stair, a chair, and think of the person you'll never meet who cut it and fitted it. Then think of someone you know who works with their hands, a plumber, a cousin who fixes things, a parent who built something once, and let a plain thank-you take shape. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.

Your line: builders. Kirat can be as small as a straight nail. Until tomorrow.

1323.title: Beyond caste names
1323.hook: Singh and Kaur were meant to replace caste surnames
1323.howItsDone: Sikhs who take Amrit receive the names Singh or Kaur; some use them alone, and some families also keep a clan or village name, which Sikhs discuss openly among themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, craftsmen and builders: Ramgarhia Sikhs, and the honest bread of Lalo the carpenter. Your line was builders.

A form on a screen. First name. Last name. The second box is doing more work than it looks. In a lot of places, a last name quietly tells a stranger where your family comes from, what your great-grandparents did for a living, sometimes which well they were allowed to drink from. This week has met Sikh communities known by a trade, a region, a history. A question sits under all of them: what happens to the second box when a Guru hands everyone the same name?
screen: `FIRST NAME. LAST NAME.` → `WHAT A SURNAME TELLS A STRANGER.` → `THE SAME NAME FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Begin at Anandpur, a story this path has told before. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh called for heads, the five who stood up came from different families and trades, and after the Amrit each was given the same name: Singh for the men, Kaur for the women who took Amrit. In a world where a surname announced your caste, one shared name meant nobody could read your birth off it. Second, the root under the name. Long before Anandpur, Guru Nanak had chosen a side. In a line from the opening pages of the Granth, in paraphrase, he keeps company with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to keep up with the great. Where the lowly are cared for, there the gaze of grace falls. A shared name is that line turned into a habit. Third, the honest part. Names didn't stop at Singh and Kaur. Some Sikh families still carry a caste or clan name after them, and you've met communities this week who are still known by one. Some Sikhs drop the surname and go by Singh or Kaur alone. Some add a village. Some keep the family name for a passport and leave it off everywhere else. Sikhs argue about this among themselves, and the argument itself shows the old ideal is still alive. Last, a name is the first thing anyone learns about you. Two shared names make a stranger ask you something else first.
screen: `AT ANANDPUR, ONE NAME FOR FIVE.` · `NANAK STANDS WITH THE LOWEST.` · `SURNAMES CAME BACK, AND SIKHS ARGUE.` · `A STRANGER HAS TO ASK SOMETHING ELSE.` · then, large: `ONE NAME FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Say your own last name silently, and ask what it tells people before you've said a word: a country, a family, a religion, a class, a story. Some of that you may be proud of, and some you never chose; hold it gently, without judging. Then let the name go for a few breaths and just be the one breathing, resting on Waheguru if you pray.
Beyond caste names. Singh and Kaur, given to every Sikh who takes Amrit, so that a surname would no longer tell anyone a person's caste. Today's word.
Your line: one name for all. A name can open a door instead of closing one. See you tomorrow.
